Equality Texas endorsed Hinojosa, Talarico and other Democratic candidates down the ballot in the Lone Star State. "We're looking cautiously optimistic to see what can be accomplished in this new legislative landscape," the group said earlier this month following the elections.

articles.title: Senate GOP takes risky bet on Dems as holiday shutdown deadline looms: 'It's a gamble'
articles.summary: Senate Republicans are betting on Senate Democrats to avert another government shutdown as Democrats aim to use funding to end the eight-month Iran war.
articles.body: Congress is nearing the deadline to avert a government shutdown, and Senate Republicans are taking a leap of faith as the clock ticks: trusting Senate Democrats to dodge a holiday disaster. When the upper chamber returns on Nov. 30, there will be just shy of two weeks for both sides to reach an agreement to thwart another partisan closure. At the center of the issue is the Iran war: Democrats intend to use the government’s purse strings to bring the eight-month conflict to an end. Republicans, meanwhile, want to put together an emergency supplemental funding package with hundreds of billions of dollars dedicated to the military, munitions and war effort. They have, for now, pressed pause on ramming those tax dollars through the party-line budget reconciliation process, and instead are opening the door to work with Democrats. DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN There’s history here: Senate Democrats have twice now ushered in a government shutdown. And though Republicans agreed behind closed doors to move forward with their counterparts, they know it’s a leap in the dark. "Each side is a gamble," Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital. "I mean, obviously, if it's partyline, when you look at the House side, you know, we got members not showing up," he continued. "So, either way, it's a gamble. It’s a toss-up whether we try to do [appropriations] or reconciliation." There is a middle ground beginning to form, however. Senate Democrats are aligning behind a plan that would fund several of the GOP’s and administration’s defense priorities, particularly refilling dwindling munitions stocks that have taken a hit from the war. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., who has been working with a small group of Senate Democrats to produce a plan, said that while they want funding prohibitions for the war, there are some exceptions, like "defense of U.S. troops if the president seeks an authorization, evacuation of U.S. personnel." SENATE REPUBLICANS PLAN 54-DAY BLITZ TO PUSH TRUMP'S AGENDA BEFORE DEMOCRATS SEIZE POWER Those exceptions would likely ride on a short-term continuing resolution (CR) that would keep the government open into early next year. He acknowledged that it was a give-and-take with Republicans, given that they do want up to $350 billion in emergency supplemental funding for the war and Pentagon, and that some limited agreements on guardrails for Iran war funding could be used as a bargaining chip for broader funding through the emergency package. "I think there's a pretty wide recognition on both sides of the aisle that some of the munitions replacement money is needed pretty soon," Kaine said. "It's not like it produces weaponry soon, but you kind of have to start it soon." MORE THAN HALF OF SOME US WEAPONS STOCKPILES USED IN IRAN WAR, RAISING CONCERNS ABOUT CHINA THREAT Others in the caucus, like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., are firm in their position that the war must end. "This is an illegal, unconstitutional, and horrific war," Sanders told Fox News Digital. "I want that — the American people want to see it ended as soon as possible." And Republicans are all too familiar with the recent history of record-shattering shutdown after record-shattering shutdown. Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital that, boiled down, the issue was about "supporting our troops and investing in our military." "I would think the Democrats would want to support that," Banks said. "I find it baffling that they're not willing to. So I hope they'll come to the table in the interest of keeping America safe and supporting our military." Turning to the normal government funding process, or at least using a CR, instead of reconciliation could pay off for Republicans down the line, too, when Democrats take control of the Senate next year. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., balked at Democrats’ recent history of shutdowns and told Fox News Digital that "if you always assume the worst-case scenario, the worst case scenario is always gonna happen." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He argued that Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and appropriators should be given a chance "to say, look, we know we have areas of controversy, but some of this … spending is very, very important." "At least try that, because then you're laying the groundwork for maybe some bipartisan regular order appropriations next year if you go down this path," Tillis said. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has been keyed into the ongoing negotiations, and said that there was "some interest, as you know, probably on our side" in striking a deal with the Democrats. When asked if it was a proposal President Donald Trump could support, Thune said, "I hope so."

articles.title: Nation’s largest grocery chain cuts thousands of jobs — sparks fury over who it’s hiring instead: 'Insanity'
articles.summary: Kroger faces backlash over cutting 3,000 U.S. jobs while recruiting for a new Bangalore hub, as critics accuse the grocer of offshoring American roles.
articles.body: Kroger, the largest traditional grocery chain in the nation, is facing strong blowback on social media over its plan to slash 3,000 jobs in the United States while advertising new positions overseas in India. The controversy comes as the Cincinnati-based grocer begins executing a three-year plan it has previously announced to cut $5 billion in costs as part of a restructuring that will eliminate roughly 37% of its U.S. corporate workforce by 2029. While Kroger maintains the reductions are aimed at lowering shelf prices through technology and leaner operations, simultaneous recruiting for a new hub in Bangalore has fueled online accusations that the company is offshoring American jobs while asking shoppers to bear high food prices. "‘They’re doing the jobs Americans don’t want to do,’" Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during President Donald Trump's first term, posted on X. "No. They are taking jobs from Americans because it’s cheaper for corporations to hire foreigners." KEY AMERICAN INDUSTRY SEEING BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM AS TRUMP'S RE-SHORING POLICIES PAY OFF In an interview with Fox News Digital, Wold said situations like this need to "start to be an honest conversation about penalizing businesses that take jobs and send them overseas." Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) responded on X by saying, "Hire American." "This insanity has to stop," retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson posted on X. "Reshore ALL US companies. We’re rapidly becoming India, and I didn’t serve 20 years defending that!" FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS "Kroger says these cuts are to ‘lower prices,’" workforce intelligence researcher Amanda Goodall wrote on X. "Classic. Do you think we will see lower prices at the grocery stores? I'm not holding my breath. I'm not a boycott person... but... damn. " In a statement, a Kroger spokesperson said the notifications "are part of the corporate headcount reduction the company announced in early October to lower prices and improve the shopping experience by simplifying operations and better use of technology." Kroger declined to answer questions regarding how many U.S. roles are being shifted to its new Bangalore capability center, the projected headcount in India or which departments were most affected. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The first wave of layoff notices went out to corporate employees last week, marking the initial phase of an overhaul announced in October by CEO Greg Foran that will pare Kroger’s white-collar workforce from roughly 8,200 to 5,200. Frontline store and warehouse employees are not targeted by the cuts. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In an October internal memo announcing the 3,000-role reduction, Foran pointed to expanding artificial intelligence and workflow automation as a central driver for trimming corporate overhead. At the same time, job boards have listed nearly 30 corporate openings for Kroger’s new Global Capability Center in Bangalore across finance, supply chain, real estate and data analytics. Chief Financial Officer David Kennerley previously told investors the overseas capability center would deliver modest savings in 2026 before generating more substantial cost reductions in 2027 and 2028.

articles.title: Trump's NVIDIA power play opens Pandora's box Democrats could weaponize, analyst warns
articles.summary: Eric Schiffer says Trump's push to reinstate NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang opens a Pandora's box Democrats may exploit, but national security won.
articles.body: The Trump administration’s efforts to re-instate Jensen Huang as CEO of NVIDIA have set a new bar for shaping a private corporation, according to Eric Schiffer, chairman and CEO of Reputation Management Consultants, a crisis management and brand protection firm. "Trump came in to really give a second life to Jensen, where he would have been dead," Schiffer told Fox News Digital on Tuesday. Schiffer said the intervention has opened a kind of Pandora’s box that Democrats may seek to exploit to benefit ideological allies in the private sector. Still, he said the national security interests underpinning Trump’s efforts to intervene on behalf of Huang fall within the responsibilities of the presidency. JENSEN HUANG'S NVIDIA RETURN SENDS CHINA A CLEAR MESSAGE: THE AI RACE IS ON Asked whether he believes Democrats may use the moment as a precedent to tip the scales in favor of ideological allies down the road, Schiffer said he sees that possibility in the cards. "I think that, of course, they would have that capability. I think that that is a risk," Schiffer said. But Schiffer said the justification would likely depend on the circumstances. "If the Democrats had a similar situation or it's a leading organization that is so critical to both national security and the economy, then it would make sense," Schiffer said. "However, if the Democrats — and perhaps the future president that might be a Democrat — is empowering a crony… then I think they're going to be open to significant criticism. And I think that there would be pushback on behalf of the American public," he added. "This is very unique and different in my opinion." CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN NVIDIA's board decided to bring back CEO Jensen Huang after he resigned earlier this month following reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom The New York Times reported U.S. intelligence identified as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset operating under corporate cover. A source familiar with the matter told Fox News that President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance worked over the weekend to reinstate Huang after they received security briefings and became convinced that Huang did not present a national security threat in his role as CEO. In recent days, Vance worked with figures in Silicon Valley and executives at NVIDIA to urge the board to reinstate him, the source said. Onlooking Democrats have blasted Trump's involvement, hailing it as a presidential overreach. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, noted that Trump owns NVIDIA stock. Trump holds between $13 million and $62 million in NVIDIA stock, according to reporting from the Washington Post and its review of Trump's disclosures. "We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions," Garcia said in a statement. U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-Calif., echoed Garcia's criticisms. "We will not allow America’s national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," Jeffries wrote in a press release on Monday. Despite those criticisms from Democrats , Schiffer believes the nation’s security interests prevailed through Trump’s decision, arguing that NVIDIA’s central role in U.S. competition with China made Huang’s return a matter the president could not ignore. "[In] the office of the presidency, you know, there's the duty to ensure that the United States continues to be strong geopolitically and certainly from a national security perspective. The move to help Jensen accomplishes those," Schiffer said. "That's part of what a good leader and a strong leader should be doing," he added. TO BEAT CHINA ON AI, WASHINGTON MUST FIRST EARN AMERICANS' TRUST Apart from its reasoning for the administration's intervention, Schiffer pointed out that Trump had only used soft power to encourage Huang's return — a far cry from forcing NVIDIA into its decision through any formal use of the presidency. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This was not a situation where the government came in under some military policy and tried to take control of NVIDIA," Schiffer said. "This was the lightest form of power." The White House and the office of the Vice President did not immediately respond to requests for comment about whether they shared concerns about Democrats using political power to intervene in the private sector in future administrations or whether the administration had created a new precedent for corporate intervention.

articles.title: Marco Rubio's 2028 stock surges among House Republicans as Trump insiders split on Vance
articles.summary: House Republicans are pushing Secretary of State Marco Rubio to launch a 2028 presidential run, calling him the GOP's unifier after midterm losses.
articles.body: As Republicans continue to pick up the pieces from their 2026 midterm losses, one Trump administration official is catching some GOP lawmakers' eyes as the party's next great hope. "[Secretary of State Marco Rubio] is the whole package. He's intelligent, charismatic, level-headed, cool-tempered, and very knowledgeable about the issues and eloquent in explaining them," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "I think there is a lot of interest from Republicans in seeing him explore a run." Indeed, multiple House Republicans who spoke with Fox News Digital said they and their colleagues are pushing Rubio to run for president in 2028. The Cabinet official himself has publicly dismissed any talk about his future political plans, but his name is on the rise among Republicans who have said the party needs to pivot from the issues that cost them votes in November. HOUSE CONSERVATIVE EMERGES WITH 2028 PRESIDENTIAL PICK AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'I AM ALL IN' "Now that we lost majorities, we can't push policy, so we will have to do better at communicating," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital on election night. "I am all in for Marco. He can be a unifier." They're notable comments coming from the Indiana Republican, who was among the founding members of the conservative House Freedom Caucus. MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028 Rubio has long been held up as a potential 2028 contender, despite a previous unsuccessful White House bid in 2016. He and Vice President JD Vance have been regarded as the top contenders for the GOP nomination, but it's Rubio's name that has come up in conversations among House Republicans, Fox News Digital was told. GOP MIDTERM BLOODBATH EXPOSES CRACKS IN VANCE'S 2028 WHITE HOUSE AMBITIONS "A number of my colleagues, unsolicited by me — they come up with me, knowing that I'm on board, [from] Miami, et cetera — and said that they'd want to support him, that they would support him if he ran," Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. " And it's not just a few. There's a number, a pretty good number, that have told me that." Gimenez said he supported Rubio even before the election. The same goes for Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., who told Fox News Digital he's been openly backing his fellow Florida Republican for two months. "And I think the affirmation that I'm getting from talking to people is overwhelming," Haridopolos said. "He is not only understanding what's happening today, but our place in history. And I think his inspirational story, his parents coming from Cuba and living the opportunity that is America, and inspiring people that anything is possible, is the uplifting message we need." SEC MARCO RUBIO: THE WEST FORGOT WHAT MADE IT GREAT. WE MUST REDISCOVER OUR ROOTS BEFORE WE LOSE THEM Both Haridopolos and Malliotakis pointed to Rubio's recent speech in Greece calling for the renewal of Western civilization as an example of his presidential possibility. Those remarks, set in Athens, were widely lauded for their scenic backdrop of the Acropolis at sunset. And Malliotakis, who is half Cuban herself, said Rubio could "reach" Hispanic voters who largely turned away from the GOP in November. LATINO VOTERS SWING BACK TO DEMOCRATS AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS: POLL "The potential for him to be the first Hispanic president is huge for our party and the country," she said. But within the administration itself, it appears no clear successor has emerged. One source familiar with talks told Fox News Digital that Trump administration staffers were "about 50/50" when asked if they favored Vance or Rubio. "I think it’s pretty split," one administration official said. "I don’t think the president really knows. I think if you asked him today, he’d say Rubio." "50/50 feels right to me," a second administration official said. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly referred Fox News Digital to Trump’s previous comments on the matter. Over the weekend, Trump told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that Vance and Rubio are "doing fantastically" and are "both very, very popular" when asked who he would like to see run on the Republican and Democratic tickets ahead of the 2028 presidential election. articles.title: Trump traded competence for blind loyalty — America is paying the price
articles.summary: The core problem runs deeper than the cascade of indefensible decisions flowing from a directionless White House. The real crisis, as always, is Trump himself.
articles.body:
The mismanagement roiling Donald Trump’s White House over the past week will come as no surprise to the millions of Americans who booted Republicans out of office en masse earlier this month, but the sheer scope of this administration’s incompetence still beggars belief.

It’s hard to imagine how things could get worse for a presidency that managed to derail the economy , decimate Republicans’ congressional majorities and post record-low approval ratings all in the span of just two years. Yet after a week that saw Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defend his taxpayer-funded getaway to a football game as a public service, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. cost America its measles elimination status and Trump effusively praising Russian dictator Vladimir Putin as “ my friend ,” it’s clear MAGA has found a way to lower the bar even further into the dirt.

Now Trump can also add a troubled stock market to his grim list of crises, as the NASDAQ , S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average reached correction territory las week before rebounding. Financial markets tanked in large part due to investor fears over an AI bubble that Trump’s policies and social media pronouncements recklessly inflated at every opportunity. Regular Americans’ retirement funds may pay the price, even as Trump cashes out up to $148 million , thanks to more than 750 well-timed stock trades in September alone.

The roughly 70 percent of Americans who are struggling to make ends meet amid a historic affordability crisis have enough on their plate without the added headache of babysitting Trump and his feckless advisers. Millions of Americans are facing their second straight Thanksgiving of rising food costs . The price of a turkey jumped nearly 25 percent this holiday season , thanks in part to Trump’s fixation on deporting the migrant workers who make up the backbone of America’s poultry processing industry. Nearly everyone in the country is paying more for less, and it’s doubtful they feel very thankful for the privilege.

Before Trump can even begin to get his administration back on track with the American people, he’ll need to make some serious staffing changes. He should start with Mullin, whose nightmarish performance during the Federal Aviation Administration’s recent nationwide ground stop ought to have been immediately disqualifying but who has managed to cling to power due to his unquestioning personal loyalty to Trump.

In a moment when the people needed clarity and reassurance from the Department of Homeland Security, Mullin offered a dissembling mess of responses that amped up anxieties while offering nothing in the way of answers. In his first press conference after the FAA’s order, Mullin nervously declared that the halt was “ not another 9/11 ” before adding ominously — and vaguely — “ I don’t want to say this is a crisis, but it is .” Mullin spent the next few days cycling through even more unconvincing answers for the outage. By the end of the week, Mullin’s dissembling had earned him a mocking new title: “ Secretary of Imprecision .”

One big problem with dumping senior officials, however, is the lack of qualified candidates willing to risk their reputations and job security to work for a White House known to demand loyalty instead of honest guidance. Another problem is Trump’s new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, the ruthlessly ambitious MAGA true believer who has been known to destroy the careers of those who try and moderate Trump’s worst impulses. Few serious policy experts would pass Miller’s purity testing, and even fewer would want to submit to his ideological inspection in the first place.

Mullin’s gaffes may be enough to force him out, but Trump is loath to part with officials when he is already facing a seriously depleted talent pool. That means the bar for public conduct is even lower than it was in Trump’s first term, and slavish personal loyalty has now become most officials’ most effective shield against accountability. Knowing that, is it any surprise that Trump’s second term seems to be stuck in neutral, swirling the political drain two full years before he leaves office?

Trump’s willingness to accept incompetence is one of the main reasons why America voted Republicans out from office earlier this month. But the core problem runs deeper than the cascade of indefensible decisions flowing from a directionless White House. The real crisis, as always, is Trump himself.

Until Republicans can acknowledge that fact, Americans will continue to live in a nation where economic and national security uncertainty are norms, not outliers. Our country deserves better than two more years of that chaos.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies.

articles.title: The midterms haven’t changed the Supreme Court
articles.summary: Supreme Court picks have political consequences.
articles.body:
Since President Trump retook office in January 2025, hundreds of millions of people across the globe have watched helplessly as the U.S. system of government succumbed to cruelty, corruption, chaos and incompetence. The midterm elections operated as a sort of defibrillator for democracy, sending a much-needed message that individual agency still exists in America. Voters reminded elected officials that they have power to decide the terms under which American society is governed.

But one thing the midterms did not and could not do was change the U.S. Supreme Court, which has revealed itself to be a dangerously anti-democratic institution. This, of course, is by design. The court itself has reiterated many times that “[a] fundamental principle of our representative democracy is … that the people should choose whom they please to govern them.”

But the Framers chose a different model for the judicial branch, which is instead appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate. In Federalist No. 78 , Alexander Hamilton defended the configuration of what he called the “least dangerous” branch, arguing that their jobs for life would enable judges to make decisions without fearing removal by voters in retaliation for unpopular rulings. In No. 79 , he said that barring Congress from reducing their pay was also important because a “power over a man’s subsistence amounts to a power over his will.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

In theory, federal judges are nonetheless beholden to the voters through the appointment and confirmation process. Supreme Court picks have political consequences. In 2016, Trump ran for office on a promise to populate the Court with justices willing to overrule Roe v. Wade. After Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization came down, stripping women and girls of the right to abortion, campaign strategists reportedly called the ruling a “massive vulnerability for Republicans.”

In his concurring opinion, Justice Brett Kavanaugh justified the majority’s unmistakable callousness by punting to women’s access to ballot-casting in state elections (never mind the powerlessness of girls too young to vote). The issue of abortion, he wrote, “will be resolved by the people and their representatives in the democratic process in the states or Congress.”

Yet for other issues around which Americans are deeply divided, the justices have grabbed for themselves the power to decide what’s best for rest of the 343 million who live among them. Bear in mind that when the Court rules on the meaning of the Constitution, that operates like an amendment. Every other public actor in the country, including members of Congress, state and municipal legislators, and even voters via ballot referendum, is bound by what the justices say the Constitution’s ambiguous text means.

Consider the Second Amendment, which states: “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” From 1939 to 2008 , the Supreme Court interpreted this language to mean that the Constitution does not protect the right to keep and bear an unregistered short-barreled shotgun without evidence of a reasonable relationship to a well-regulated militia. It was up to voters and legislators to decide whether and how to limit individual possession of firearms for purposes of public safety.

Prior to the 2008 decision in District of Columbia v. Heller, therefore, federal gun laws gradually expanded, culminating in a federal assault weapons ban enacted in 1994. That law expired in 2004, leaving it up to members of Congress — and their constituents — to decide whether to replace it.

That choice ended when the court decided in Heller that the Second Amendment was not limited to the needs of a militia. It instead means, Justice Antonin Scalia explained for the majority, that an individual has a immutable constitutional right to possess guns in certain circumstances — in that case, a handgun in the home for self-defense — and that legislatures and voters are powerless to overstep that new boundary, even in the name of public safety.

Think about it: After reading the Second Amendment one way for nearly a century, the court shifted gears. An issue left to the democratic process became a red line established by unelected judges with jobs for life. Whether Miller or Heller is the “better” reading of the Second Amendment is beside the point. The issue that every American should think about is who should get to decide such a life-threatening question: unelected judges or the people at the ballot box?

On December 2, the justices will hear oral argument in a consolidated case in which they chose to decide whether state and local governments can ban civilian ownership of AR-15s and other semiautomatic rifles under the Second Amendment. If five justices say no, gun safety voters and their descendants will be left further out in the cold. If the high court declares constitutional protection for AR-15s, no number of mass shootings or dead school children will authorize voters to collectively decide to make America safer.

That’s not to say the new Congress is powerless to make voters heard. Through simple legislation, it can change the court’s configuration or its jurisdiction to hear these kinds of cases.

For the time being, it’s up to the people to demand the power to decide for themselves whether deadly machines have more rights in America than human beings capable of pregnancy. That means demanding that Congress remind the justices of their proper role in a democracy: No more kings.

Kimberly Wehle is currently a fellow at the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study in the Humanities and Social Sciences and author of “How to Read the Constitution — and Why,” as well as “What You Need to Know About Voting — and Why” and “How to Think Like a Lawyer — and Why. “

articles.title: Welcome to the steroid era of scientific discovery
articles.summary: Without a doubt, the results obtained using GenAI have been impressive, solving problems that would have taken years, if not decades, for people to solve independently. But where artificial intelligence can provide answers, humans no longer have the vital comprehension gained through the struggle of finding the solution.
articles.body:
Not so long ago, performance-enhancing drugs indelibly altered the record books of Major League Baseball. Today, generative AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT are doing much the same with knowledge discovery and research output, creating inventories of research results and manuscripts that can be produced orders of magnitude faster than humans can peer-review them.

While most people use generative AI to answer basic questions, draft letters and interpret documents, researchers have enlisted the technology as a collaborative partner, working with AI in mathematics, computer science and engineering to identify solutions to unanswered problems that have been open for years.

A candidate solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Problem reported by OpenAI is but one such example. They deployed 10,000 algorithmic agents to tackle this problem, generating a 166-page proof that left the mathematics community with the unenviable task of deciphering the details, attempting to confirm what the software produced and what data was used to produce it .

More recently, an Anthropic mathematician claimed to resolve the Riemann Hypothesis . OpenAI has also published results for open mathematics and computer science problems, while expanding its ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program by making its software tool available at no cost to up to 200,000 faculty researchers and their students.

But even when formal proof assistants are used to verify formal proofs, machine validation does not automatically translate into human understanding. What’s more, the cost to identify the candidate solution to the Navier-Stokes Problem has been estimated to be as high as $15 million , far above the $1 million prize that a successful result would garner. This suggests that while GenAI may be capable of solving open problems, the cost of doing so is steep.

Without a doubt, the results obtained using GenAI have been impressive, solving problems that would have taken years, if not decades, for people to solve independently. But where artificial intelligence can provide answers, humans no longer have the vital comprehension gained through the struggle of finding the solution.

Some may compare this shift to the arrival of electronic calculators or symbolic math software . Those tools automated routine computation, permitting researchers to focus on more advanced reasoning. GenAI, however, automates the reasoning itself. Working through the mathematical process is akin to weightlifting for a bodybuilder. When dumbbells labeled 200 pounds weigh just two pounds, the lifter gains little benefit. GenAI may permit more problems to be explored, but the cognitive struggle needed by young researchers to develop research discovery skills is never exercised.

Accelerating output barely scrapes the surface of this disruption.

Young researchers will be forced to adapt to this new model for discovery, harnessing the very best features of GenAI to conduct their research. For those working in academia, criteria for promotion will need to be revamped, since output alone will no longer be an appropriate measure for achievement. This may involve pivoting to oral interviews that permit peer cross-examination to ensure that researchers understand the breakthroughs obtained with their digital collaborators. Indeed, much like how baseball players hit 60 or more home runs in a season during the steroid era, generating reams of research manuscripts through collaboration with GenAI will not only be common, it will become expected. It will also challenge the peer-review process, as vetting massive volumes of manuscripts will overwhelm even the most efficient journal operations.

As GenAI compresses the discovery timeline, it will create a real-time race between what machines can generate and what humans can digest and understand. Much like the physical limits of Moore’s Law on microchip design, constraints around data access and computing power will inevitably slow this acceleration. How long that takes remains to be seen, though it is likely measured in years, if not decades.

This is indeed the steroid era of knowledge discovery. The one difference between this era and baseball’s is that no researchers will be banned from participating. But as we observe the cascade of candidate breakthroughs, we must ask ourselves: If GenAI does all the heavy lifting, what happens when human intellect loses its muscle?

Sheldon H. Jacobson, Ph.D., is a professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He applies his expertise in data-driven risk-based decision-making to evaluate and inform public policy.

articles.title: Fulton County ordered to turn over copies of 2020 ballots
articles.summary: A Fulton County, Ga., judge ordered the county to turn over copies of ballots seized by the FBI in a raid earlier this year to the State Election Board, a Republican-run board with election oversight authority. Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe of the Fulton County Superior Court said the county must turn over ballot copies on…
articles.body:
A Fulton County, Ga., judge ordered the county to turn over copies of ballots seized by the FBI in a raid earlier this year to the State Election Board, a Republican-run board with election oversight authority.

Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe of the Fulton County Superior Court said the county must turn over ballot copies on a flash drive to the board, denying its motion to block a previous order.

A Fulton County spokesperson declined to comment on a pending legal matter.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The county must turn over the records by 5 p.m. Wednesday, and the judge limited who was able to view them. The judge’s order does not directly specify the reason the records must be turned over.

The move comes as Republicans, led by President Trump, continue to relitigate the 2020 election results in Georgia and specifically in Fulton County, home to most of Atlanta. The president has said for years that the election in Georgia was stolen in 2020 without evidence and despite multiple recounts affirming former President Biden’s win.

The FBI raided Fulton County in January, seizing 2020 election ballots as part of an investigation into alleged “irregularities.” A judge later ruled that the government could hold onto those ballots despite Fulton County’s efforts to have them returned. No charges have been filed.

The agency deemed the Fulton County case a priority investigation and moved to allocate hundreds of agents to the investigation.

The 2020 election in Georgia was overseen by Republicans, but top officials drew Trump’s ire when they refused to overturn Biden’s win despite the president’s urging for officials to find more Trump votes.

Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger was stripped of his authority to oversee elections by the Georgia Legislature the following year. While the secretary of state previously chaired the State Election Board, he was removed from the board entirely as part of a sweeping 2021 election law.

The overwhelmingly Democratic Fulton County has been at odds with the president since the election. District Attorney Fani Willis indicted Trump on racketeering and conspiracy charges in 2023 related to actions after the 2020 election. Willis was ultimately removed from the case, and the charges were dropped once Trump returned to office.

articles.title: Trump is sabotaging his own Iran sanctions strategy
articles.summary: If Washington wants whistleblowers to come forward, it must stop undermining the reasons they might.
articles.body:
Only Washington could set out to help both victims of terrorism and whistleblowers who expose sanctions evasion by terrorist regimes — and somehow wind up pitting the two against each other.

First, credit where it’s due: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has repeatedly urged insiders to expose the financial networks that help Iran evade American sanctions.

“This is your chance,” he declared in September, promising potential rewards regardless of “where you live or who signs your paycheck.” Months earlier, Bessent promised that “Treasury will reward whistleblowers” who expose sanctions violations. That’s good policy, in addition to being the right thing to do.

Yet that very same day, Bessent’s department proposed regulations that would eliminate these promised rewards in many cases — even when a whistleblower helps the government recover millions of dollars.

The contradiction is striking. Washington is asking people to risk their livelihoods, careers and even safety to help enforce U.S. sanctions, while at the same time pushing rules that could deny these whistleblowers the rewards Congress intended to encourage their cooperation.

Sanctions evasion often depends on banks, trading companies, shipping firms and intermediaries that disguise where goods or money are going. U.S. investigators cannot easily obtain records of transactions deliberately concealed overseas. That’s where insiders come in. They can identify the shell companies, falsified invoices, hidden customers and executives who approved the schemes.

But a whistleblower who exposes misconduct may never work in the industry again. Financial awards help make those risks worth taking and provide a means to mitigate their effects.

Consider Everett Stern, an HSBC Bank compliance officer who reported suspicious financial transactions to U.S. authorities after his internal warnings went unheeded. HSBC subsequently paid $1.9 billion to resolve sanctions and money laundering violations. Stern says his decision to speak out effectively ended his banking career.

Congress understands this reality, which is why it established a Treasury whistleblower program offering eligible insiders 10 to 30 percent of the monetary penalties collected in qualifying enforcement actions. The Justice Department has a separate corporate whistleblower program that also covers sanctions violations.

But both programs are now colliding with another important federal initiative: the U.S. Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund . Congress created the fund to compensate Americans harmed by terrorist attacks, and it has distributed billions to victims and their families. Its mission is essential.

The conflict arises because Congress also directed that 75 percent of proceeds from certain civil sanctions violations, and all proceeds from covered criminal violations, go to the victims’ fund. That money should continue reaching terrorism victims. But Treasury’s proposed regulations would go further, excluding those transfers when calculating whistleblower awards.

Suppose a whistleblower’s tip enables the government to collect a $10 million civil penalty for violations of sanctions on Iran. Because $7.5 million must go to the victims’ fund, Treasury’s proposal would count only $2.5 million toward the whistleblower’s award. At the maximum 30 percent rate, that reduces a potential $3 million award to $750,000.

Nothing about the whistleblower’s contribution changed. The government still recovered $10 million. Terrorism victims still receive $7.5 million. Yet the incentive for taking the risk to expose the misconduct has shrunk by three-quarters. For smaller penalties, the result is worse. After the transfer, if the remaining sum falls below $1 million, a whistleblower’s award eligibility is eliminated altogether.

The Justice Department faces a similar problem. In August, a federal appeals court ruled in Englehardt v. Blanche that the law requires proceeds from a sweeping array of criminal sanctions offenses to be sent to the victims’ fund. Under the Justice Department’s whistleblower guidelines , that transfer may wipe out the proceeds used to determine whether an award is available. Here, too, a multimillion-dollar recovery could produce no whistleblower award.

The irony is that weakening whistleblower incentives could ultimately hurt terrorism victims. Many sanctions violations are discovered only because insiders come forward. Fewer disclosures will mean fewer investigations, fewer penalties and ultimately less money flowing to the very victims Congress wanted to help.

The two groups should not be pitted against each other by ill-advised policy choices. They share an interest in exposing more violations and collecting more penalties.

This problem is fixable without diverting a single dollar from terrorism victims. The government can calculate an award using the full qualifying enforcement recovery, transfer every dollar legally owed to the victims’ fund and pay the whistleblower separately from other legally available money in federal award funds.

The Justice Department can do this by revising its program guidelines. Treasury should adopt the same principle when it finalizes the regulations for its whistleblower program. And if the statute that created Treasury’s program ends up preventing that, Congress should make a targeted amendment. In either case, terrorism victims would receive every penny the law promises them.

The administration is right to enlist insiders against Iran’s sanctions evasion networks. But those people need more than promises that vanish in the fine print. If Washington wants whistleblowers to come forward, it must stop undermining the reasons they might.

Ari Yampolsky is a founding partner of Whistleblower Partners LLP .

articles.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) said in a new interview that former President Biden should have put more effort into reining in Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu amid the war in Gaza. Shapiro expressed support for the alliance between Israel and the U.S. in an interview published Tuesday with The Wall Street Journal; however, he…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) said in a new interview that former President Biden should have put more effort into reining in Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu amid the war in Gaza.

Shapiro expressed support for the alliance between Israel and the U.S. in an interview published Tuesday with The Wall Street Journal ; however, he also said that the Israeli prime minister must face accountability because of his conduct in the Gaza war.

“I don’t think that either the current president or President Biden used the leverage of the United States of America effectively to make sure that the weapons were being used in ways that comport with American values,” Shapiro told the Journal, discussing the war in Gaza.

Biden has faced criticism from the left over how he handled the war in Gaza, with progressives saying the administration should have placed more pressure on the Israelis over their conduct in the war, which has resulted in a humanitarian crisis.

In the last few years, the issue of American aid for Israel has become more prominent amid the Gaza war, which followed the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel that killed more than 1,000 Israelis. Since then, tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been killed in Israel’s war. Some have labeled Israel’s actions in the war as a genocide.

In this year’s midterms, multiple Democratic candidates expressed disdain for Israel’s actions in Gaza, with some, like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), pushing to cut off aid to the Middle Eastern country.

Over the summer , Democrats in the House split almost down the middle on an amendment to cut off American aid to Israel. The amendment, led by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), was seen as a doomed show vote. However, it provided a test for Democrats who had faced heat from the activist base over Israel.

The Hill has reached out to the White House over Shapiro’s comments on President Trump.

articles.title: The Pentagon’s ‘heat ray’ weapon is not an acceptable form of border control
articles.summary: Imagine a toddler having its skin burned by the heat ray, and it’s easy to understand why even a test of this technology at the border is alarming.
articles.body:
In a surprising piece of news that has flown under the radar, the Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a heat ray weapon for potential use along the southern border.

Known as the Active Denial System , the weapon uses invisible energy beams to cause a burning sensation on human skin. The heat ray is powerful enough to reach more than half a mile away and triggers an immediate instinct to flee. On Fox News last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said , “any technology that we can use to deter people from trying to enter this country illegally, we’re doing that.”

While the heat ray is described as non-lethal, its possible use raises serious safety, legal and logistical concerns. Authorities have repeatedly declined to use such technology on enemy combatants, prisoners and protesters. Military-grade weapons should not be turned on migrants at the border.

Military officials in the past have compared the impact of the Active Denial System to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. This description seems to minimize its effect. Journalists who have volunteered to experience the heat ray describe it as brutally painful, calling it “intolerable” and like “a wall of scorching heat.” And while the weapon has been tested on military personnel and hardy volunteers, it is unclear if it has ever been tested on pregnant women, children, people with disabilities or the elderly — all of whom might be found among migrants along the border.

Imagine a toddler having its skin burned by the heat ray, and it’s easy to understand why even a test of this technology at the border is alarming. Physicians for Human Rights notes that the ray could damage blood vessels, nerves and glands , and that its long-term impact remains unknown.

Deploying the Active Denial System along the border would be legally problematic, too. Under U.S. and international law, all migrants have the right to claim asylum and other forms of humanitarian relief. Using the heat ray to prevent people from doing so would thus likely be illegal. It’s hard to envision any way that the heat ray could be lawfully used against people approaching the border, as that would involve harming people before they took any illegal action. What’s more, the heat ray is on the UN Special Rapporteur on Torture’s prohibited equipment list . Its deployment along the border would probably amount to an infringement upon Mexico’s sovereignty as well.

The Active Denial System is a logistical question mark, because it has never been used in real-life settings. Its effects are based on use in controlled situations by properly trained personnel. It’s notable that military commanders decided against using the weapon in Afghanistan in 2010, and that former Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen refused to authorize its use at the border in 2018. As recently as 2020 , the first Trump administration rejected the idea of turning the heat ray on protesters in Washington. Now Homeland Security wants to use migrants at the border as guinea pigs for this dangerous weapon?

Meanwhile, illegal crossings along the southern border are at the lowest level since 1970. Daily border apprehensions have plunged 94 percent from the Biden era, according to administration officials. This all begs the question of why we need a heat ray weapon deployed there at all.

In a statement , Customs and Border Protection said it is “continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities.” But there is not enough evidence that the heat ray weapon will achieve either of these goals. And just because technology is non-lethal does mean it is appropriate to use against people. Then again, the possible use of the heat ray is on brand for an administration whose cruelty towards immigrants appears to know no bounds .

With Democrats winning control of the House this month, lawmakers must demand hearings on any planned tests or deployment of the Active Denial System at the border. And they can bank on public support, as 58 percent of Americans disapprove of the administration’s approach to immigration . One broader question is whether any test of the heat ray could open the door to it being used domestically, on American citizens exercising their constitutional right to protest.

A heat ray is too unsafe and risky to be deployed for border control. Weapons designed for war should never be used against civilians.

Raul A. Reyes is an immigration attorney and television commentator in New York City.

articles.title: Trump wishes Robert Pattinson ‘luck’ as James Bond
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday said he wishes actor Robert Pattinson “luck” as he embarks on his new role as the seventh actor to portray British spy James Bond. “He looks nice. You know, I wish him luck,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, according to the New York Post. He called out to adviser…
articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday said he wishes actor Robert Pattinson “luck” as he embarks on his new role as the seventh actor to portray British spy James Bond.

“He looks nice. You know, I wish him luck,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, according to the New York Post .

He called out to adviser Natalie Harp to bring him articles about Pattinson, asking her if the character of Bond is “conservative,” the outlet wrote. Harp replied that he’s “been good.”

“I always like people that like me,” the president replied.

One of the printouts was an October 2012 post on the social platform X, then called Twitter, where Trump lamented Pattinson’s breakup with fellow “Twilight” actor Kristen Stewart.

“Robert Pattinson should not take back Kristen Stewart. She cheated on him like a dog & will do it again—just watch. He can do much better!” he wrote at the time.

The president told reporters, “That was a long time ago.”

Pattinson and Stewart had rekindled their relationship after the latter was photographed kissing the director of her film “Snow White and the Huntsman,” Rupert Sanders. The director was married at the time when Trump posted on social media to the “Batman” actor. Stewart later apologized.

Trump wrote about Pattinson several more times around the premiere of “The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn –– Part 2,” the final film in the “Twilight” franchise. One post took a jab at former President Obama, as he “dumped” the controversial Rev. Jeremiah Wright “like Robert should dump” Stewart.

By the time of the last “Twilight” film’s release, the then-businessman wrote he hoped “Robert Pattinson will not be seen in public with Kristen –– she will cheat on him again!”

The actor later told Entertainment Weekly that it was “surreal” knowing that the author of the posts had since become president .

Stewart also referred back to the posts during a “Saturday Night Live!” monologue in February 2017 , saying that the incident “for some reason … made Donald Trump go insane” and adding that she thought he was “in love with my boyfriend.”

“Donald, if you didn’t like me then you’re really probably not going to like me now, because I’m hosting ‘SNL’ and I’m, like, so gay, dude,” Stewart said.

Amazon MGM Studios announced last week that Pattinson will play the latest iteration of Agent 007 in the 64-year-old film series.

First portrayed by Sean Connery in 1962’s “Dr. No” and most recently portrayed by Daniel Craig in 2021’s “No Time to Die,” Pattinson will star in Amazon’s first Bond film since acquiring MGM Studios in 2022, with the “Dune” trilogy director, Denis Villeneuve, at the helm .

Pattinson has been in a slew of films since his “Harry Potter” and “Twilight” days, recently playing “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen in the A24 film “Primetime.” He is slated to appear next month as the villain Scytale in “Dune: Part Three” next month and again as the Dark Knight in 2028’s “The Batman: Part II.”

articles.title: We’re paying hunters to kill wolf pups. Washington is about to make it worse
articles.summary: We are living through a biodiversity crisis created not by wolves but by human decisions.
articles.body:
In late April, in northern Idaho, hunters killed 12 wolf pups — at least one entire litter wiped out in or near its den. They were paid for it .

Three hunters received $2,000 per pup — $24,000 in total — through a state-backed reimbursement program run with the Foundation for Wildlife Management. It reimburses not only ammunition and traps, but fuel, outdoor clothing and even truck payments for scouting, hunting and trapping wolves.

Idaho allows this because it allows almost everything when it comes to wolves. Under its 2026-2027 rules , wolves can be hunted year-round — even in spring, when newborn pups depend on their parents — with no daily or seasonal limit on how many wolves one person may kill.

This is not an outlier. It is a pattern, and it is spreading.

In Alaska, the state has authorized another trapping season for a wolf population its own scientists describe as isolated, inbred and genetically vulnerable.

The fall estimate for wolves in Game Management Unit 2, which includes Prince of Wales Island, is 187 animals , with a range of 125 to 279 — already below the Board of Game’s newly adopted objective of 200 to 300 wolves . Yet trapping begins Nov. 15 and runs through Dec. 15, with hunting already underway since Sept. 1. Recent 31-day seasons there have taken 45 to 74 wolves — a quarter to 40 percent of that estimate.

A 2025 genomic study found these wolves the most inbred of the Southeast Alaska populations examined, comparable to the Isle Royale wolves that suffered severe inbreeding depression.

In Montana, hunters had killed 39 wolves by Nov. 2. The statewide quota is 300 this season, down from 458 last year, after a new estimate showed far fewer wolves than previously thought. Meanwhile, the Ninth Circuit heard arguments on Oct. 13 on whether the Fish and Wildlife Service must reconsider its finding that Northern Rocky Mountain wolves do not need federal protection. No ruling has been reported yet.

And in Washington, a deadline is coming that could make all of this worse. On Sept. 4, President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing the secretary of the Interior to determine within 90 days whether gray wolves and Mexican wolves have met the criteria for delisting or downlisting under the Endangered Species Act . That 90-days runs out in early December.

The order does not itself remove protections, but if the secretary determines the criteria have been met, the administration is directed to begin delisting or downlisting them — and to encourage states to remove protections and revise rules for killing wolves to protect livestock.

Consider Mexican wolves: 319 of them in Arizona and New Mexico, after a decade of steady recovery. Under the Fish and Wildlife Service’s most recent recovery plan, one downlisting scenario requires an average of at least 320 wolves over four years. We are being asked to decide their fate on a margin of one wolf.

Wolves are not interchangeable. They are family-based, cooperative animals. A 17-year Oregon study found that packs losing a parent were nearly five times more likely to dissolve, almost 16 times more likely to fail reproductively and recruited 66 percent fewer pups. Killing a pup does not only remove a pup. Killing a parent can rupture an entire pack — and paying people to do it turns that rupture into a business model.

The defense, in state after state, is familiar: Populations are stable, harvests are sustainable, managers can adjust later. But that is sustained extraction wearing the language of stewardship. A population is deemed healthy if it can absorb human killing, while ecological function, social structure and genetic security are treated as secondary.

In Idaho, the state’s own plan called for reducing the population to about 650 animals in spring. It nevertheless remained above 1,100 this year, down from a peak of about 1,600 in 2019. The killing continues anyway.

Washington should ask before that December deadline, why authorize another substantial harvest, and why pay for killing pups, when the best estimates are already below the state’s own conservation objectives for isolated and inbred populations? Interior should publish its full analysis before any delisting decision — population data, genetic-risk analysis and the science on pack stability. And Congress should ask, in public, what recovery means if it ends with fewer wolves, broken packs and public money for dead pups.

We are living through a biodiversity crisis created not by wolves but by human decisions. Habitat destruction, fragmentation, extraction and the repeated removal of species that hold ecosystems together. Restraint is now an essential act of conservation.

Wolves do not need us to assign them a purpose. They already have one. Our obligation is to stop dismantling those communities and calling the destruction management — and to stop paying for it.

Christine Villabona-Kuntz is a registered nurse, environmental writer and animal advocate .

articles.title: Democratic senator demands ‘action plan’ to regain measles elimination status
articles.summary: Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) is demanding the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to produce an “action plan” to regain measles elimination status in the U.S. after the country lost its long-standing distinction last week. On Nov. 17, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced rising measles cases had cost the U.S. its…
articles.body:
Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) is demanding the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to produce an “action plan” to regain measles elimination status in the U.S. after the country lost its long-standing distinction last week.

On Nov. 17, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced rising measles cases had cost the U.S. its elimination status, which it had maintained since 2000. In a Tuesday letter to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Democrat demanded his office release an agenda by Jan. 24 outlining the department’s plans to earn back the title and fight the ongoing measles outbreak.

“At a minimum, the plan should include the corrective action plan HHS sends to PAHO, as well as specific steps and a timeline to interrupt measles transmission, the federal resources available to states and how states can request them, how CDC will track and report measles cases and deaths, and any additional resources HHS needs from Congress,” she wrote.

There have been a total of 5,838 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with state health agencies reporting additional cases. This is more than double the 2,289 cases reported in 2025 alone.

Blunt Rochester, who sits on the Senate Health Committee, accused the Trump administration official of erasing “decades of public health achievement” during his two years in office.

“In your time as Secretary your dangerous actions have created chaos and contributed to growing confusion around the safety and efficacy of vaccines,” she wrote, citing leadership changes at HHS, adjustments to the country’s vaccine recommendations and a measles outbreak under his watch.

After the U.S. lost its measles elimination status, PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa emphasized the group’s commitment to “working with every country” to regain the distinction.

“We know what works. We have done it before. And with sustained commitment and action, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again,” Barbosa said in a statement .

HHS press secretary Emily Hilliard told The Hill on Wednesday the department had received Blunt Rochester’s request and would “coordinate with the requesting committee accordingly.”

articles.body:
The Army detonated a degraded stockpile of lead-based munitions in Iowa early Wednesday, proceeding with the controlled explosion despite the public health fears that initially pushed back the plans.

The Army has argued the controlled detonation at the Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, was necessary to avoid an unintended explosion.

In statements offered two hours after the detonation, Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley called the detonation “tremendously successful” and said mitigation efforts “reduced as close to zero” the risk to people in the region.

Because of the resulting plume of lead azide particles, the Department of Health and Human Services called on children, pregnant people and chronically ill people Tuesday to evacuate the area .

Bad weather, high prices and continued tech outages have also caused roadblocks for Americans traveling over the Thanksgiving weekend. President Trump on Tuesday re-upped the administration’s push for more funding and staffing for air traffic control.

Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO earlier this week has sparked continued scrutiny. The embattled tech mogul reportedly apologized to his staff this week and acknowledged he was in therapy after multiple extramarital affairs were exposed.

The scandal has drawn renewed attention to chips exports and China. The president has not ruled out a pardon.

Meanwhile, Washington is empty as lawmakers are on recess. Trump and first lady Melania Trump are also spending the remainder of the week in Florida.

articles.title: Cenk Uygur blames Israel for Jensen Huang debacle — what?!?
articles.summary: If you know Cenk, you can probably guess where he’s going with this, but if not, please enjoy the surprise.
articles.body:
Well, it’s been quite the week, with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang miraculously returning from the dead, so to speak, to return in triumph to the company he founded — in no small part thanks to President Trump, who vouched for him to the board.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you probably know that Huang stands accused of having an affair with a Chinese spy, although the evidence that she was actively spying is not all that persuasive, and the federal government says there’s no evidence Huang’s actions have jeopardized national security. You make take that with a grain of salt if you wish.

But we should be pretty satisfied that the reason for Huang’s initial resignation is exactly what it looked like: News broke of this affair, which appeared to suggest that Huang had put his board in a difficult position and possibly compromised the company and the country, to the benefit of China.

Enter Cenk Uygur of “The Young Turks,” who has a different culprit in mind. If you know Cenk, you can probably guess where he’s going with this, but if not, please enjoy the surprise.

Israel did it! They took Huang out! Or they put him back in? Either way, it’s Israel. If we don’t know what’s going on, Israel. If there’s anything we don’t understand, Israel. Israel, Israel, Israel.

Am I allowed to call this a derangement syndrome of sorts? I know this is a favorite hobbyhorse of the far left, and also, to be fair, some on the far right. But it’s just getting silly at this point. No, I don’t believe that what happened to Huang was orchestrated by Israel, on either end. I think it was orchestrated by Huang being very careless. If there was a country or government at fault, it’s not Israel, it’s China. Quite obviously.

Moving on, according to The Wall Street Journal , Alice Huang, the woman who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, had ties to Chinese intelligence, but — and this is important — quote: “There was no smoking-gun intelligence proving she had been actively tasked with collecting information on Jensen Huang or passing along national-security secrets, they said.”

Maybe her mere connection to Chinese intelligence sounds damning to you, but keep in mind that because China is a one-party autocratic state, business leaders are required to stay in contact with the government and the two are not easily untangled. That doesn’t make Jensen Huang’s behavior less reckless, but it does undermine the notion that this was some well-formulated plan and that state secrets were shared.

As I mentioned yesterday, the markets are super happy that Huang is back, as are his employees, who cheered his return. Democrats are less enthused, and have vowed to investigate this matter when they have congressional power come January. And I say that’s fine, because this is a very, very important thing to get right.

I would like to know exactly what, for instance, Secretaries Marco Rubio and Scott Bessent were thinking when they apparently tried to warn Trump that Jensen might be compromised. Did Trump overrule them, or was the evidence just not that compelling?

Whatever the case may be, I am willing to bet we will not discover intelligence that this was Israel’s doing. Sorry if that breaks anybody’s brains!

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.summary: Plus: Abrego Garcia arrives in Spain {beacon} It’s Wednesday and Thanksgiving eve, one of the busiest U.S. travel days of the year. If you’re at the airport, smooth travels! articles.body:
It’s Wednesday and Thanksgiving eve, one of the busiest U.S. travel days of the year. If you’re at the airport, smooth travels!

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Julia Boehning, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and jboehning@thehill.com. The 12:30 Report will return to your inbox on Monday. Happy Thanksgiving!

The Army and federal agencies appear thrilled with how a lead azide munitions blast went in Iowa on Wednesday morning.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and President Trump all provided assurances of successful mitigation efforts this morning.

FEMA administrator Cameron Hamilton said during a press conference after the detonation that “we’re finding a 0.0 detection level of lead in the atmosphere.”

Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley , head of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command, noted at the press conference that the detonation has “exceeded expectations” and “all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed.”

“There was no secondary explosion. There was no kickout. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Shirley continued.

Trump wrote Wednesday morning on Truth Social after the blast that “Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations.”

“The Army’s controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success. The threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated,” acting Army Secretary Adam Telle wrote after the blast.

EPA administrator Lee Zeldin went on CNN following the blast and said there is currently “zero detection” of lead at this point on the agency’s air sensors.

DHS, EPA and FEMA offer support: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said Wednesday morning on X that FEMA will “ensure that affected households have a safe place to stay and to address critical needs like transportation, water and meals.”

“We are using every available federal resource to protect Iowa residents,” FEMA wrote on X . “At the direction of [President Trump] and [Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin], FEMA is working with the @USArmy and federal partners.”

Surrounding states monitor: Missouri, Illinois and other states bordering Iowa are currently monitoring any possible lead exposure in the air.

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said on the social platform X that “Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained.”

Ahead of the blast, residents in Middletown, Iowa, where the blast took place, boarded windows, sealed doors or evacuated the town in preparation of lead particles being thrown into the air by the Army’s detonation.

The Trump administration is planning to place new tariffs on dozens of countries, including China and all 27 members of the European Union, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer ‘s office announced Wednesday.

The proposed levies include a 20 percent tariff on Chinese imports, as well as import taxes on goods from Cambodia, India, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and all EU members.

Greer’s office said the administration imposed the duties pursuant to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which grants U.S. trade representative the ability to impose tariffs on countries he determines conduct “unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory” trade practices “that burden or restrict U.S. commerce.”

The Section 301 strategy: The Trump administration used the Trade Act provision to impose levies after the Supreme Court struck down tariffs President Trump unveiled in April 2025 under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Doubling down: The announcement comes as Americans grapple with rising prices heading into the holiday season. Tariffs were among myriad Trump policies that proved deeply unpopular and contributed to higher costs of living, which Democrats seized on for sweeping victories in the midterms.

Meanwhile, at Mar-a-Lago: Trump is set to meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at 4 p.m. EST. The president has repeatedly criticized the military alliance, in which EU countries hold a significant majority.

The meeting is listed as closed to the press for now. Rutte went on “Fox & Friends” this morning to preview his meeting.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia , the Maryland resident at the center of one of the Trump’s administration’s biggest immigration fights, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after being self-deported on Tuesday, according to Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.).

Abrego Garcia’s arrival in Spain marks the end of a two-year long battle between him and the Trump administration. He decided to be deported to Spain after he was threatened to be sent to Africa.

According to the Associated Press, Abrego Garcia arrived in Madrid Wednesday morning and spoke with reporters before departing in a van.

Battle with the Trump admin: Abrego Garcia was mistakenly deported last year after Trump took office. He was arrested in Baltimore in 2025 and was sent to a mega prison in El Salvador.

Abrego Garcia eventually returned to the Maryland after the Supreme Court ruled the administration had to return him to the U.S.

ICE issues statement: “Kilmar Abrego Garcia departed the United States pursuant to a removal order. He paid for his own flight and received no incentives,” ICE wrote on the social platform X. “He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States.”

Relationship with Van Hollen: The senator visited Abrego Garcia in El Salvador, forming a relationship that continued back in the U.S.

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” the Maryland senator said after Abrego Garcia arrived in Spain.

💾 Trump did not rule out pardoning recently reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in an interview published Tuesday evening. The president played a personal role in the push to bring Huang back to Nvidia despite the high-profile scandal that led the tech mogul to resign earlier this month.

👪 First lady Melania Trump shared Wednesday she succeeded in reuniting nine more children with their families amid Russia’s war in Ukraine, bringing her total to 43. Russian President Vladimir Putin is accused of forcibly transferring Ukrainian children to Russia.

articles.body:
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) said in a new interview that President Trump’s selection of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff “shows his level of fear and insecurity.”

“He picked the only person around him who’s been there from the beginning, a person who he knows is undyingly loyal, won’t leak on him, won’t countermand any of his instructions,” Christie told Rolling Stone magazine in an interview published Tuesday, discussing Miller.

“Stephen Miller is comfort food for Donald Trump in a moment of crisis. He’s his teddy bear to bring to bed because he’s scared,” the former governor added.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Earlier this month, Trump announced his then-chief of staff, Susie Wiles, was exiting the White House and Miller would take up her role.

The White House chief of staff shake-up came in the wake of Republicans’ widespread defeats in this year’s midterms, with the party losing control of the House and Senate.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” he continued. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Miller is known as an immigration hard-liner and a loyalist to the president. His promotion to chief of staff was notably controversial for Democrats and some Republicans.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who will most likely be the Speaker of the House in the next Congress, called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands” after Trump’s promotion announcement.

articles.title: Alex Pretti’s mother: Family ‘still being stonewalled’
articles.summary: The mother of Minneapolis nurse Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration authorities earlier this year, said Tuesday the family is “still being stonewalled” from receiving answers about the investigation into his death. Susan Pretti wrote on Instagram that “304 days ago, the federal government murdered my first born and only son…
articles.body:
The mother of Minneapolis nurse Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration authorities earlier this year, said Tuesday the family is “still being stonewalled” from receiving answers about the investigation into his death.

Susan Pretti wrote on Instagram that “304 days ago, the federal government murdered my first born and only son Alex.”

“It has been 32 days since our press conference when we begged the DOJ [Department of Justice] and Daniel Rosen in the U.S. Attorney’s office to do their jobs, we are still being stonewalled,” she continued.

“Alex will never again be at our Thanksgiving table,” she wrote. “We will never hear his infectious laughter, nor his funny stories of camping, biking, time spent with his beloved friends, or even some of his most heartbreaking stories of his patients’ struggles.”

Susan Pretti told the DOJ and Rosen, the U.S. attorney for the District of Minnesota, that as they gather with their families for the holiday, “remember Alex and what your actions have stolen from us and continue to take from us every single day since Jan. 24, 2026! We will never stop seeking justice for Alex.”

She and her husband, Michael, last month accused the DOJ of protecting those responsible for his death and have received no communication from federal officials in the nine months since his death.

“Share the evidence now so prosecutors can follow the facts and hold these men accountable,” Michael Pretti said. “Do your job and stop shielding Alex’s killers.”

Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, was killed Jan. 24 while filming immigration officers during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota. His death came less than three weeks after Renee Good, another Minneapolis resident and U.S. citizen, was shot and killed during an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operation.

The Hennepin County, Minn., medical examiner in February ruled that Alex Pretti died by homicide .

The family and Minnesota officials have also said the DOJ had stopped sharing evidence in connection with the deaths of Alex Pretti and Good. State officials asked a judge to order the DOJ to hand over the evidence it has, adding that the federal government has no legal authority to obstruct the investigation.

The DOJ agreed to share evidence with state officials in July after the department was sued for the evidence, but the cooperation stopped soon after.

The family has also criticized the Department of Homeland Security for failing to retract its initial characterization of Alex Pretti, claiming he had intended to “do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement” — an account contradicted by video footage of the encounter.
